abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel information-theoretic framework for understanding emergent coordination in large-scale multi-agent systems, fundamentally departing from traditional reductionist approaches that analyze individual agent behaviors in isolation. Existing theories struggle to capture the collective dynamics that arise when hundreds or thousands of autonomous agents interact. We introduce the concept of collective information manifolds, which characterize the global coordination landscape through topological invariants that remain invariant across agent implementations. Our theoretical analysis reveals that emergent coordination exhibits phase-transition-like behavior, with sharp transitions between disordered and coordinated states governed by information-theoretic thresholds. We formalize the conditions under which micro-level agent behaviors give rise to macro-level coordination patterns, establishing rigorous proofs that connect local interaction rules to global system properties. The framework provides testable predictions about coordination emergence that we validate through extensive multi-agent learning simulations involving up to 10,000 agents. This paradigm shift from analyzing individual agents to studying the information geometry of the collective offers fundamentally new tools for designing and predicting multi-agent system behaviors, with implications for social simulation, swarm robotics, and distributed AI more broadly.

We address a fundamental limitation in multi-agent negotiation theory: the assumption of unbounded rationality that underlies most equilibrium concepts. Real-world autonomous agents operating in dynamic environments must make decisions under severe computational and temporal constraints, yet existing solution concepts fail to adequately capture the strategic implications of bounded rationality. This paper extends the classical Nash equilibrium framework through a unified bounded-rational equilibrium concept that incorporates explicit models of agents' reasoning capabilities. We prove that this new equilibrium notion subsumes existing approaches as special cases while providing strictly more predictive power in realistic scenarios. Our theoretical analysis establishes convergence properties and characterizes the efficiency loss induced by cognitive limitations, yielding novel bounds on the price of boundedness. Furthermore, we develop a polynomial-time algorithm for computing approximate bounded-rational equilibria in normal-form games that significantly outperforms existing methods. The framework is applied to analyze bilateral negotiation scenarios between autonomous agents with asymmetric reasoning capabilities, revealing strategic behaviors that Nash-based analyses completely miss. These theoretical contributions advance both game theory and agent decision-making research by providing tools that bridge the gap between normative equilibrium theories and the practical constraints of autonomous agent design.

This paper introduces MetaSynth, a novel agent architecture that fundamentally reconceptualizes the relationship between symbolic reasoning and reactive control in autonomous agents. Existing architectures typically treat deliberation and reactivity as separate modules that must be carefully balanced, leading to brittleness when encountering unexpected situations. MetaSynth instead implements a unified cognitive architecture where symbolic planning and reactive behaviors emerge from the same underlying computational substrate through a process of compositional abstraction. The architecture employs a hierarchical representation scheme where concrete sensorimotor routines are progressively abstracted into symbolic plans through experience-driven synthesis. We present the complete system design, including the composition operators, abstraction mechanisms, and runtime synthesis algorithms that enable continuous adaptation. Implementation in a robotic agent demonstrates competent performance across manipulation, navigation, and human-robot interaction tasks without manual task-specific programming. Crucially, the architecture enables agents to generalize learned reactive behaviors into symbolic planning knowledge and vice versa, creating a virtuous cycle of capability improvement. Empirical evaluation shows that MetaSynth agents exhibit robust performance under distribution shift, handling novel situations through adaptive composition of known primitives. This paradigm shift from architecture-as-engineered to architecture-as-synthesized opens new directions for agent-oriented software engineering.

We present CoordX, a significantly improved coordination protocol for distributed multi-agent teams operating in time-critical domains. While existing coordination mechanisms achieve reasonable performance, they suffer from high communication overhead, brittle dependency structures, and poor scalability. CoordX introduces three key innovations: (1) a hierarchical commitment protocol that reduces communication complexity from O(n²) to O(n log n) while preserving coordination guarantees, (2) a predictive coordination algorithm that anticipates team members' needs based on learned behavioral models, and (3) a fault-tolerant commitment recovery mechanism that gracefully handles agent failures without disrupting team objectives. The protocol is designed within the standard agent communication paradigm, ensuring compatibility with existing agent platforms. We provide a complete implementation integrated with the Jason agent development framework, enabling straightforward adoption by practitioners. Extensive evaluation in simulated disaster response scenarios involving 50+ heterogeneous agents demonstrates that CoordX achieves 40% faster mission completion compared to state-of-the-art coordination approaches while reducing communication bandwidth by 60%. The protocol exhibits graceful degradation under communication latency and agent failure conditions that cause baseline methods to catastrophically fail. This work advances multi-agent learning and coordination research by providing both theoretical coordination guarantees and practical implementation that scales to real-world deployment scenarios.
